displayQuote: Permit me to issue and control the money of a nation, and I care not who makes its laws

meta.title: Who really said "Permit me to issue and control the money of a nation"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mayer Amschel Rothschild. No letter, diary, speech or newspaper record exists. The earliest printed version, in 1908, names nobody; the Rothschild credit first appears in 1935, 123 years after he died, in a book of financial conspiracy theory.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Permit me to issue and control the money of a nation'?
meta.ogDescription: No source exists. The line is unattributed in 1908 and only pinned on Mayer Amschel Rothschild in 1935 — 123 years after his death. A British publisher cut it from a memoir in 2024.

answer.label: Nobody — no source of any kind exists
answer.authorDates: Unattributed in print by 1908 · credited to Rothschild only from 1935
answer.sourceLine: There is no Rothschild source — no letter, ledger, diary, speech, memoir or newspaper report. Mayer Amschel Rothschild died in 1812. The earliest located printing of the saying, in 1908, attaches it to no one in particular; the first version naming him appears in 1935, in Gertrude M. Coogan’s Money Creators, with no citation. The dates later attached to it range from 1790 to 1863 — several of them after he was dead. This line is a staple of antisemitic conspiracy writing, and the plain factual answer is that it has no documented origin at all.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Let us control the money of a country and we care not who makes its laws.
trail: The earliest form anyone has located in print is from 1908, and it names no author — it is vaguely credited to ‘the money lenders of the Old World.’ That is the shape of a slogan, not a quotation the trail ↗.

The wording on this page, with a named author attached, first appears in 1935, in Gertrude M. Coogan’s Money Creators — a book arguing that the world is run by international financiers. Coogan gives no source and no date. Everything since traces back through her.

The tell is the dating. Repetitions since 1935 have assigned the remark to 1790, 1838, 1863 and other years, most of which fall after Rothschild’s death in 1812. A real quotation acquires one date; an invented one acquires many.

The nearest thing to an ancestor is a genuine and unrelated line from Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun, writing in 1703 about ballads — let me write a nation’s songs and I care not who writes its laws. The financial version reads like that proverb with the money swapped in.

In April 2024, after the writer Dorian Lynskey spotted it in Liz Truss’s memoir Ten Years to Save the West, the publisher Biteback apologised and removed it from future editions the 2024 correction ↗.
source.excerptNote: The earliest located printed form, from 1908. It is credited to no individual, it is plural, and it is less quotable than the version that circulates now — all signs of a slogan that was later sharpened and given a famous name.

author.name: Mayer Amschel Rothschild
author.heading: Why his name got attached
author.metaLine: 1744–1812 · German banker, founder of the Rothschild banking family
author.bio: Mayer Amschel Rothschild (1744–1812) was a coin dealer and banker in the Frankfurt Judengasse who built a family firm his five sons extended across Europe. He left a large paper trail — ledgers, business correspondence, a will — and this sentence appears nowhere in it. His name was attached in 1935, more than a century after his death, by an author writing about hidden financial control, and the line has circulated ever since as shorthand for a conspiracy theory rather than as anything he said. Treating it as a quotation gives a fabrication the dignity of a source.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one is not a close call, and it is worth being blunt about why it matters. The sentence has no source, and the name was added a century after the fact by a writer arguing that bankers secretly run the world.

items.why: No letter, diary, speech, ledger entry or contemporary report. He died in 1812; the first printing that names him is from 1935 and cites nothing the trail ↗.

The commonest date given is 1838 — twenty-six years after he died. Others place it in 1863, half a century after. When a quotation collects several incompatible dates, none of them came from a document.

A shorter variant — give me control of a nation’s money and I care not who makes its laws — is often pinned on the London son instead. That version has no source either; swapping generations does not create evidence.

Fletcher genuinely wrote that whoever makes a nation’s ballads need not care who makes its laws. That is a remark about culture and popular feeling. The money version reads like a later rewrite of a proverb everybody already knew.

The line is circulated as proof that a Jewish banking family secretly controls governments. In April 2024 a British publisher apologised and cut it from a former prime minister’s memoir once its origin was pointed out. Correcting the attribution is not pedantry here; the quotation is the whole of the evidence, and it does not exist the 2024 story ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No Rothschild ever said this on any surviving record. The saying is unattributed in print by 1908 and acquires his name only in 1935, in a book of financial conspiracy theory, with no citation offered the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It offers a single lever that explains everything. If one family controls the money, then elections, parliaments and laws are theatre — and you no longer have to understand central banking, bond markets or any of the genuinely complicated machinery that decides who gets credit and who does not.

That is also what makes the missing source consequential rather than merely untidy. The sentence is usually produced as evidence, the confession that proves the case. Take away the document and there is no confession, only a slogan that somebody attached a famous banker’s name to in 1935.
detailsBody: 1703: Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun writes the genuine ballads-and-laws remark that the money version appears to be modelled on.
1812: Mayer Amschel Rothschild dies in Frankfurt, leaving substantial business papers and a detailed will. The sentence appears in none of them.
1908: the earliest located printing, in a plural form, credited to no individual.
1935: Gertrude M. Coogan’s Money Creators prints the familiar wording and attaches Rothschild’s name, without a citation.
April 2024: after the writer Dorian Lynskey identifies it in Liz Truss’s Ten Years to Save the West, the publisher apologises and removes it from future editions.
context.pull: A real quotation acquires one date. This one has acquired 1790, 1838 and 1863.
